instructions: Make the batter first. In a large bowl, stir together the 1 cup milk, 1 cup water and the 1/2 tsp salt. Whisk in 2 cups of the flour a little at a time, then keep whisking for 1 to 2 minutes, until it's completely smooth with no lumps.

Add 2 of the eggs and whisk until the batter is one even color. It should be smooth and pourable but coat a spoon, a little thicker than milk. If it runs off the spoon like water, whisk in more of the flour 1 tbsp at a time, up to the last 1/4 cup. Cover it and put it in the fridge while you get everything else ready.
Make the sauce. In a small bowl, stir the 2 tbsp doubanjiang, 2 tbsp hoisin, 1 1/2 tsp sesame oil and 1 1/2 tsp water together until smooth.
Cut the 8 egg roll wrappers in half, so you have 16 pieces.

Pour the 4 cups oil into a medium heavy pot. It should come no more than halfway up the sides. Heat it over medium high. You're heating it to 350°F, so if you have a thermometer, clip it to the side. No thermometer? Drop in a scrap of wrapper. It's ready when it bubbles right away and floats.

Fry the wrapper pieces 2 or 3 at a time, holding them flat with tongs, for 20 to 30 seconds, until the underside is light golden. Flip them and cook the other side for 45 to 60 seconds, until they're golden brown. Stand back a little. They'll spatter.
Lift them onto a wire rack or paper towels and let them cool completely. Turn off the heat under the oil and leave it to cool.
Meanwhile, slice 6 oz of the sausage (half the package) on an angle into 1/4 inch pieces. Put them in a large cold nonstick skillet, off the heat.

Set the skillet over medium and cook the sausage for 2 to 3 minutes, tossing now and then, until the edges crisp and most of the fat has melted out. Transfer the sausage to a plate and pour the fat into a small bowl.
While the sausage cooks, cut half the cucumber into thin matchsticks, thinly slice the green onions and coarsely chop the cilantro.
Wipe out the skillet and set it over medium high. When it's hot, wipe a thin layer of the sausage fat over it with a folded paper towel. When the fat runs out, use a little of the cooled frying oil.
Stir the batter. Pour about 1/2 cup into the middle of the pan and tilt and swirl the pan right away, so it spreads into a thin round.
Crack 1 egg onto the crepe and break it up right away with a spatula. Spread it out to the edges. Cook it for about 30 seconds, until the egg has mostly set.
Flip it and cook the egg side for about 10 seconds. Flip it back so the egg is on top.

Spread about 2 tsp of the sauce over the egg. Scatter a line of green onion and cilantro across the middle. Add a few pieces of zha cai, some cucumber and an eighth of the sausage next to it. Lay 2 of the wonton crackers, stacked, just below the fillings.
Fold the bottom edge up over the crackers and keep rolling it up to the top edge. Transfer it to a cutting board and cut it in half.
Cook the other 7 the same way, greasing the pan each time. If the crepe browns before the egg sets, turn the heat down a little.
Serve them hot, with the chili crisp at the table.
method_notes: Joshua Weissman's version leads now. Asian Inspirations, which led before, is rated 3.7 from 24 ratings and Tasting Table 2.9 from 63, both under the 4.0 a version needs to lead, and no version found had 20 or more ratings at 4.0 or higher, so the first version read that isn't rated low leads. The recipe now follows Weissman: a smooth batter of flour, milk, water and egg in place of the rested rolled dough, a sauce of doubanjiang, hoisin and sesame oil in place of sweet bean sauce and chili bean sauce, and fried egg roll wrappers, crisp Chinese sausage, cucumber and zha cai rolled up inside. It's halved to 8 crepes and uses his note for a 12 inch pan (smaller crepes, one egg each), with the chili crisp at the table.
